verdict: OK to lend in Kochi ship repair — back the mid-sized repair and marine-services borrowers riding the CSL-Drydocks World JV, structure against milestone cash flows, and stay away from pure shipbuilding subcontractors whose margins are guided down to 10%-12%.
title: Kochi Shipbuilding & Repair: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**Ship repair is a yard-and-dry-dock business: a vessel comes in, you sell dock time, steel, paint, machinery and skilled labour, and you get paid on completion or milestone.** Cash sits in work-in-progress on hulls under repair and in receivables from shipowners and managers, not in inventory. Shipbuilding is the opposite — long construction cycles, progress payments, heavy capex on docks and cranes. **Kochi's anchor is Cochin Shipyard, whose order book has crossed ₹21,900 crore, of which ship-repair orders are about ₹1,200 crore [2].** That single number tells you the repair pie is real but still small relative to build work.

## What has changed now
**The structural news is the 50:50 JV between Cochin Shipyard and Drydocks World for the International Ship Repair Facility in Kochi — the first public-private partnership of its kind in India's ship repair sector [1][3].** The ₹970 crore ISRF can handle repairs for up to 82 mid-sized vessels annually, and a new ₹1,800-crore dry dock is designed for aircraft carriers and Suezmax vessels [2]. **But the peer result is a warning: Cochin Shipyard guided FY27 EBITDA margin to around 14% versus 24% in FY26, with shipbuilding at 10%-12% and ship repair at 22%-24% [5][6].** Repair is the better-margin business — Q1FY26 repair revenue grew 157.2% YoY to ₹629.6 crore at 59% of total, with EBITDA margin at 22.6% [4]. **So when a proposal lands, check whether the borrower's revenue is repair-linked or build-linked; if it is a shipbuilding subcontractor, ask for the margin pass-through clause in the contract.**

## Where the growth is
**Pursue marine-service SMEs that feed the repair cluster: painting and blasting contractors, steel fabrication for repair, engine and machinery overhaul shops, electrical and automation retrofitters, and manning/labour contractors with documented dock access.** Also pursue suppliers to the JV's international fleet flow. **Avoid pure shipbuilding subcontractors and single-client fabrication units** — their margin is being guided down to 10%-12% [6]. **If a borrower's order book is one yard and one vessel, ask for the second customer before sanction.**

## How to grow safely
**Structure repair-linked lending as short-tenor working capital against assigned receivables or milestone bills, not term loans for yard capex.** Take monthly: repair-order pipeline with vessel names and dock slots, billed-versus-collected statement, and ageing of shipowner receivables. **Covenant a minimum repair-revenue share and a receivables-days cap; if collection days stretch past the agreed cap, convert the limit to a secured overdraft against bills.** The data pack gives no Kochi-specific repair credit numbers — collect from customer.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch for a borrower whose order book is entirely shipbuilding subcontracts, or whose receivables are concentrated in one shipowner or one yard.** Also watch dock-slot utilisation at the ISRF and any delay in the JV's ramp-up. **If a borrower reports falling repair share or rising unbilled WIP, cut the limit and ask for the vessel-wise billing schedule.**

## Local news versus peer results
**The JV and order-book items are local Kochi news from September 2026 [1][2][3]; the margin guidance is peer company disclosure from the same month [5][6][7].** The rating sources [8]-[11] carry no shipbuilding content and are not relied on. **Kochi-specific repair credit data is thin — lean on first principles and the peer numbers above.**
